explanation: [[kw:Term insurance]] provides coverage for a specified period (e.g., 1, 5, 10, 20 years).

discoveryHook.scenario: Rick offers Bob a 20‑payment life policy. Bob pays premiums for only 20 years, but the coverage lasts his lifetime. explanation: [[kw:20‑payment life]] provides permanent protection with premiums paid for only 20 years; after that, the policy is paid‑up.
[[kw:20‑year endowment]] pays the face amount to the insured if they live 20 years, or to the beneficiary if they die within the 20 years. It combines savings and protection.
Both have higher premiums than straight life because of the shorter payment period or endowment feature.
Endowment policies are less common today due to tax law changes.
[[imp:Paid‑up insurance means no more premiums are required, but coverage continues.]]

formulaCard.title: Cash Value and Nonforfeiture
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Reduced Paid-Up Face} = \frac{\text{Cash Value}}{\text{Rate per } \$1{,}000 \text{ for paid-up insurance}}$$
notes: Cash value grows slowly in early years and increases later.
Each policy has a table of guaranteed cash values and nonforfeiture options.

explanation: [[kw:Cash value]] is the savings component of a permanent life insurance policy that grows over time.
[[kw:Nonforfeiture options]] are choices the policyholder has if they stop paying premiums:
1. Cash surrender – receive the accumulated cash value.
2. Reduced paid‑up insurance – use the cash value to buy a smaller paid‑up policy with no future premiums.
3. Extended term insurance – use the cash value to buy term insurance for the full face amount for a limited period.
[[imp:These options ensure the policyholder does not lose the entire value they've built.]]

visuals.title: Nonforfeiture Options Example
visuals.caption: These options protect the policyholder's accumulated value.

rows.1: Receive cash value in lump sum; policy ends.

Keep the full face amount as term insurance for a limited period using the cash value.

discoveryHook.scenario: After 10 years, Bob's straight life policy has accumulated a [[kw:cash value]] of, say, $5,000. If Bob wants to cancel the policy, he can take the cash. Or he can use it to buy a reduced amount of paid‑up insurance or extended term insurance. These are [[kw:nonforfeiture options]]—values that cannot be forfeited if he stops paying premiums.
